content: 1. Encourage property owners to empty overflowing but otherwise functional permanent sanitation facilities when feasible. 2. Conduct intensive hygiene promotion campaigns focusing on immediate care-seeking, handwashing with soap, safe disposal of child and infant feces in toilets, hygienic care of sick individuals and their waste, proper practices during corpse washing and burial, avoiding contact with drain water (especially for children), and treating drinking water supplies. 3. Promote and support the installation of handwashing facilities in homes and institutions. 4. In the medium term, use a combination of demand creation and enforcement to persuade owners to repair leaks, rebuild or upgrade unsafe toilets, or construct new toilets where none exist. 5. Where individual household toilets are not feasible, organize the construction of community toilets shared by defined groups of households, ensuring robust operation and maintenance systems. 6. Promote the construction of soakaways and drain fields to manage liquid effluent from on-site sanitation facilities or leaking sewer connections. If this is not feasible, organize mass desludging to increase effluent residence time in tanks and reduce solids carry-over. 7. At healthcare facilities, urgently eliminate leakages and overflows of liquid effluents, perform minor repairs, and desludge to maximize the efficiency of existing sanitation systems. 8. Ensure sanitation facilities in healthcare settings are operational, accessible to all, and equipped with nearby handwashing facilities with soap and water. 9. Review sanitation arrangements to ensure all fecal material is contained, liquid effluents are treated on-site and infiltrated into the soil or safely discharged to a sewer system connected to a treatment plant. 10. Promote the use of licensed desludging operators and temporarily suspend tipping fees if it reduces open dumping. 11. Inspect all fecal sludge management equipment and enforce rectification of faults to prevent inadequate containment or spillage. 12. Increase vigilance against open dumping of fecal sludge and enforce strict measures to ensure operators discharge at authorized sites. 13. Promote and enforce the use of disinfectants to clean serviced premises and desludging equipment, with follow-up inspections. 14. Review desludging practices with operators to minimize risks for both operators and customers. 15. Engage traditional emptiers to promote the burial of fecal sludge rather than dumping it in drains, water bodies, or open land. 16. Ensure healthcare facilities have culturally acceptable, private, safe, clean, and accessible toilets, including provisions for individuals with reduced mobility and menstrual hygiene management. 17. Patients should use bedpans only when necessary, and these should be handled safely with appropriate personal protective equipment to avoid spillage. 18. Fecal waste from bedpans and water used for washing them should be emptied into a toilet or the sanitation system through appropriate means such as a sluice or macerator. 19. Provide a reliable water point with soap near toilets for handwashing. 20. Ensure all fecal waste and greywater are fully contained. If connected to a functional treatment plant, these wastes can be combined and discharged. If no sewer is available, convey fecal waste and greywater in separate drains, treating fecal waste in an appropriately sized facility. 21. Contain liquid effluent on-site through subsurface infiltration. If this is not possible, disinfect the effluent in a baffled tank with adequate contact time before discharging it into the environment beyond the healthcare facility. 22. Never reuse liquid effluent, even if disinfected. 23. Allocate a consistent budget for the operation and maintenance of the healthcare facility wastewater system. 24. Designate a trained staff member with official responsibility for the system, supported by maintenance personnel. 25. Include wastewater system management on the infection prevention and control agenda, alongside laboratory waste, solid waste, and infectious waste management. 26. Foster behavior change at individual, household, and community levels to increase the adoption, consistent use, and maintenance of household toilets. 27. Promote handwashing with soap at critical times, the construction and use of non-emptiable pit latrines, and the regular desludging of facilities. 28. Encourage connection to sewerage systems where available and ensure safe practices in handling wastewater and fecal sludge in food production and sale. 29. Governments should lead and fund behavior change initiatives, ensuring alignment among stakeholders and robust monitoring mechanisms. 30. Health authorities must integrate sanitation behavior change strategies into all interventions, ensuring sufficient resources and coordination with infrastructure providers. 31. Maintain accurate, up-to-date information on sanitation practices through national surveys and academic studies. 32. Provide technical support for standard indicators and methods to measure behavioral outcomes, ensuring data comparability and sharing. 33. Engage organizations with technical expertise, such as universities and social marketing agencies, to design evidence-based behavior change programs. 34. Ensure sanitation behavior change efforts are evidence-based, targeted, and include feedback mechanisms for learning and adaptation. 35. Align all actors around shared behavioral objectives to reinforce efforts and avoid competition or undermining. 36. Ministries of Health should oversee sanitation behavior change strategies, set targets, develop guidelines, and manage coordination among stakeholders. 37. Ensure sanitation behavior change is part of broader public health efforts, such as cholera prevention, trachoma elimination, and reducing intestinal worm infections in children. 38. Allocate specialized staff and financial resources to sanitation behavior change, ensuring demand is created for existing services and services are used effectively. 39. Build capacity in local and regional authorities, providing tools and technical support for local programming and stakeholder relationships. 40. Understand the determinants of sanitation behaviors, including knowledge, costs, motivation, and integration into daily routines, to design effective interventions. 41. Address barriers to facility use, such as accessibility, safety, cleanliness, and distance, to promote sustained adoption and use of sanitation facilities.
